A partial answer: $L_p=\infty$ for every $p>1-1/\sqrt2\approx0.2929$, by the elementary argument below. A computer-assisted extension gives $L_p=\infty$ for $p\ge0.232$; I state that result at the end, omitting the computational details. For $0<p<0.232$ I do not know, though Einar Rødland's long simulations on MSE suggest $L_p=\infty$ for every $p>0$.

Theorem. Let $S_n$ be the sum of row $n$, with the top entry numbered row $0$. For $0<p\le1$, $$ \mathbb E S_n\ge\lambda^n,\qquad \lambda=p^2+\sqrt{p^4+4p(1-p)}. $$ Moreover, $\lambda>1$ exactly when $p>1-1/\sqrt2$.

The first $N$ rows contain $N(N+1)/2\le N^2$ entries. Thus, when $\lambda>1$, their expected arithmetic mean is at least $\lambda^{N-1}/N^2\to\infty$, proving $L_p=\infty$. At $p=1$ the bound is $2^n$, which is exact. At $p=1/2$ it gives growth factor $(1+\sqrt{17})/4\approx1.28$.

The idea. Rødland's argument discards the tails contribution: each entry is a parent twice, so the expected row sum grows by a factor of at least $2p$. To get below $p=1/2$, keep track of the tails contribution, which measures the jumps between neighbouring entries. Disagreeing coins create new jumps, so we track the sum and the total variation together.

Pad each row with zeros on both sides. Then the edge entries also follow the rule, since both the sum and the absolute difference of $0$ and $1$ are $1$. Write $$ S=\sum_j x_j,\qquad V=\sum_j|x_{j+1}-x_j|, $$ where all sums run over the zero-padded row. We have $V\le2S$, and row $0$ has $S=1$, $V=2$. Primes denote the corresponding quantities for the next row.

Step 1 (sum). $$ \mathbb E[S'\mid x]=2pS+(1-p)V. $$ Indeed, the child of $(a,b)$ has mean $p(a+b)+(1-p)|a-b|$. Summing over adjacent pairs counts each entry twice and each jump once.

Step 2 (variation). $$ \mathbb E[V'\mid x]\ge4p(1-p)\sum_j\min(x_j,x_{j+1}) =4p(1-p)S-2p(1-p)V. $$ To see this, take neighbouring children $y,z$ with parents $(a,b)$ and $(b,c)$. Keep only the two outcomes in which their coins disagree; each has probability $p(1-p)$. Using $|u|\ge u$, $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[|y-z|\mid x] &\ge p(1-p)\Bigl(\bigl|a+b-|b-c|\bigr|+\bigl|b+c-|a-b|\bigr|\Bigr)\\ &\ge p(1-p)\bigl(a+b-|b-c|+b+c-|a-b|\bigr)\\ &=2p(1-p)\bigl(\min(a,b)+\min(b,c)\bigr). \end{aligned} $$ Summing over neighbouring children counts each $\min(x_j,x_{j+1})$ twice. The final identity follows from $2\min(a,b)=a+b-|a-b|$.

Step 3 (combine). Set $F=S+tV$, where $t\ge0$. The two preceding steps give $$ \mathbb E[F'\mid x]\ge \bigl(2p+4p(1-p)t\bigr)S+(1-p)(1-2pt)V. $$ Choose $$ t=\frac{1-p}{\lambda+2p(1-p)}\ge0. $$ Since $\lambda$ satisfies $$ \lambda^2-2p^2\lambda-4p(1-p)=0, $$ the coefficients on the right are $\lambda$ and $\lambda t$, respectively. Hence $\mathbb E[F'\mid x]\ge\lambda F$. Iterating gives $$ \mathbb E F_n\ge\lambda^nF_0=\lambda^n(1+2t). $$ But $F_n\le(1+2t)S_n$, since $V_n\le2S_n$, so $\mathbb E S_n\ge\lambda^n$.

Finally, the quadratic defining $\lambda$ has one positive root and one nonpositive root. Its positive root exceeds $1$ exactly when its value at $1$ is negative: $$ 1-2p^2-4p(1-p)=2p^2-4p+1<0. $$ For $0<p\le1$, this is equivalent to $p>1-1/\sqrt2$. $\square$

A further bound. A computer-assisted extension of this argument gives $$ \mathbb E S_n\ge(5001/5000)^n \qquad\text{for every }p\in[29/125,1], $$ and therefore $L_p=\infty$ for $p\ge0.232$. It uses a potential that also tracks differences between entries two places apart and the variation of the jumps. The resulting local inequality was checked independently in exact rational arithmetic; I omit the computational details here.

These results concern the expectation, as asked. A typical triangle may grow much more slowly.

The proof was developed and checked with AI assistance.
